units.text: Opening a new database connection costs the Ledger service about 30 ms, because each one needs a TLS handshake and an authentication round trip.
units.topic: Running a shared connection pool › Why pool connections

units.text: A pool keeps a set of connections open and lends them to requests, so most requests skip that cost entirely.
units.topic: Running a shared connection pool › Why pool connections

units.text: The pool also caps how many connections the service can hold, which protects the database from a traffic spike.
units.topic: Running a shared connection pool › Why pool connections

units.text: Each Ledger instance runs a pool of at most 20 connections.
units.topic: Running a shared connection pool › Operating the pool › Sizing the pool

units.text: The database accepts 400 connections in total, and 40 of those are reserved for migrations and administrators.
units.topic: Running a shared connection pool › Operating the pool › Sizing the pool

units.text: That leaves room for 18 instances at full size, so the autoscaler is capped at 18 instances.
units.topic: Running a shared connection pool › Operating the pool › Sizing the pool

units.text: Raising the pool size only helps while requests are waiting for a connection; once the database CPU is saturated, more connections make every query slower.
units.topic: Running a shared connection pool › Operating the pool › Sizing the pool

units.text: A pool sized for peak traffic also holds idle connections at night, which costs memory on the database but nothing else.
units.topic: Running a shared connection pool › Operating the pool › Sizing the pool

units.text: A request waits at most 2 seconds to borrow a connection before it fails with `POOL_EXHAUSTED`.
units.topic: Running a shared connection pool › Operating the pool › Timeouts

units.text: The wait limit is deliberately shorter than the 5-second request deadline, so the caller still has time to return a clear error.
units.topic: Running a shared connection pool › Operating the pool › Timeouts

units.text: Each query also has a statement timeout of 3 seconds, set with `SET statement_timeout = '3s'` when the connection is opened.
units.topic: Running a shared connection pool › Operating the pool › Timeouts

units.text: The statement timeout does not apply to migrations, which run on their own reserved connections without a limit.
units.topic: Running a shared connection pool › Operating the pool › Timeouts

units.text: A long transaction holds its connection for its whole duration, so the team keeps transactions under 500 ms.
units.topic: Running a shared connection pool › Operating the pool › Timeouts

units.text: Before lending a connection that has been idle for more than 60 seconds, the pool runs `SELECT 1` to check that it still works.
units.topic: Running a shared connection pool › Operating the pool › Health checks and failover

units.text: A connection that fails the check is closed and replaced, and the request gets a fresh one.
units.topic: Running a shared connection pool › Operating the pool › Health checks and failover

units.text: During a database failover, every open connection breaks at once, so the pool is drained and refilled from the new primary.
units.topic: Running a shared connection pool › Operating the pool › Health checks and failover

units.text: Refilling is limited to 5 new connections per second per instance, so that 18 instances reconnecting together don't overload the new primary.
units.topic: Running a shared connection pool › Operating the pool › Health checks and failover

units.text: Until the pool is refilled, requests may see `POOL_EXHAUSTED` errors for up to about 4 seconds.
units.topic: Running a shared connection pool › Operating the pool › Health checks and failover

units.text: A connection that stays borrowed for more than 10 seconds is logged as a possible leak, together with the stack trace of the code that borrowed it.
units.topic: Running a shared connection pool › Operating the pool › Connection leaks

units.text: The pool does not take a leaked connection back by force, because the code holding it may still be using it.
units.topic: Running a shared connection pool › Operating the pool › Connection leaks

units.text: Most leaks the team has found came from error paths that returned early without releasing the connection.
units.topic: Running a shared connection pool › Operating the pool › Connection leaks

units.text: Leak warnings are reviewed every week, and a leak that comes back gets a ticket for the team that owns the code.
units.topic: Running a shared connection pool › Operating the pool › Connection leaks

units.text: The pool exports three gauges: connections in use, idle connections, and requests waiting to borrow.
units.topic: Running a shared connection pool › Operating the pool › Watching the pool

units.text: An alert pages the on-call engineer when requests have been waiting for more than 30 seconds in a row.
units.topic: Running a shared connection pool › Operating the pool › Watching the pool

units.text: A sustained queue usually means slow queries rather than a pool that is too small, so the runbook starts with the slowest statements, not with the pool size.
units.topic: Running a shared connection pool › Operating the pool › Watching the pool

units.text: The idle gauge drops to zero during a failover and recovers as the pool refills, which makes it a quick way to confirm that a failover has finished.
units.topic: Running a shared connection pool › Operating the pool › Watching the pool

units.text: A pool makes connections cheap and bounded, but its size, its timeouts and its failover behaviour have to be set together with the database's own limits.
units.topic: Running a shared connection pool › Takeaway
